fetched_contents.text: Effects of Ageing on Hand Function Introduction[edit | edit source] Age-Induced Hand Impairment Hand function decreases with age in both men and women, especially after the age of 65 years. Deterioration in hand function in the elderly population is, to a large degree, secondary to age-related degenerative changes in the musculoskeletal, vascular, and nervous systems. Deterioration of hand function in older adults is a combination of local structural changes (joints, muscle, tendon, bone, nerve and receptors, blood supply, skin, and fingernails) and more distant changes in neural control. These age-related changes are often accompanied by underlying pathological conditions (osteoporosis, osteoarthritis, rheumatic arthritis, and Parkinson's disease) that are common in the elderly population[1]. Hand Dexterity[edit | edit source] Hand dexterity is a term used to explain a range of different hand abilities and performances. These include reaction time; hand preference; wrist flexion speed; finger tapping speed; aiming; hand stability and arm stability. Age and grip strength are significant predictors of hand dexterity. Aiming and tapping hand dexterity (involving rapid, coordinated, goal-directed actions) is moderated by the factor of grip strength more than age i.e. hand exercises may improve particular types of hand dexterity. [2] Musculoskeletal Hand Problems in Older Adults[edit | edit source] * Musculoskeletal hand problems are common in the population aged over 50 yrs. * Hand function seems to remain stable until age 65 years, after which it gradually reduces. * Prehension pattern selection did not seem to differ with age. * Statistically significant differences in age were found for prehension pattern frequency, hand strength, and performance time. * After age 75 years, age differences in performance are apparent.[3] * Most are painful and have a significant impact on everyday life. * Women that are very old are especially vulnerable to the effect of hand problems on their daily activities.[4] Factors Affecting Function in Aging Hands[edit | edit source] Extrinsic Factors[edit | edit source] * Environmental factors (ultraviolet radiation, chemical irritants) * Physical activities (work-related, recreational sports, and hobbies) * Nutrition * Traumatic injuries Intrinsic Factors[edit | edit source] * Genetic factors * Endocrine factors * Metabolic disorders * Diseases (osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, osteoporosis) Pathological Changes[edit | edit source] * Soft tissues (muscles, tendons, blood vessels, nerves) * Hard tissues (bone, hyaline cartilage, fingernails)[1] Muscles[edit | edit source] One of the most common changes in aging skeletal muscle in the body is the major reduction in muscle mass ranging from 25% to 45%, i.e. “Sarcopenia of old age”[5]. The diminished muscle strength of the aging hand is attributed to decreasing muscle mass. There are 11 intrinsic muscles and 15 extrinsic hand muscles with direct functional roles in the hand. * There is a significant reduction in both action potentials and in the number of viable motor units associated with the hand muscles in the elderly. * Extrinsic and intrinsic hand muscles produce the force required for gripping objects (grip force). * After 60 years of age, there is a rapid decline in hand-grip strength, by as much as 20–25%, accompanied by a substantial loss of muscle fibers and decreased muscle-fiber length, particularly in the Thenar muscle group. * The thumb intrinsic musculature constitutes approximately 40% of the total intrinsic musculature of the hand.[6] * Three of the main thumb muscles play important roles in stabilizing the thumb during strong pinch grips of objects and these commonly show age-related dysfunction. * The contractile capacity of the Thenar muscle in elderly people has been assessed finding higher muscle fatigue resistance in older adults, attributed to differences in both the PNS and CNS.[1] Tendons[edit | edit source] Tendons are composed of dense connective tissue, primarily formed by densely packed, orderly arranged, collagen fibers. * Tendons have a very poor blood supply and are virtually avascular in the regions of tendon insertion[7]. * The primary function of tendons is to attach muscles to bone and to transmit muscle force to the skeletal system with limited stretch or elongation. * Changes due to aging cause reduced microcirculation of the synovial sheaths of the tendons and tendons unit, causing difficulties in the ability to adapt to environmental stress, decreased range of joint motion, and decreased flexion. This may also cause flexion contractures of the overlying joints. * The tensile strength of tendons is a measure of elongation of the tendon during tensile testing, the ultimate tensile strength values for aged tendons decrease by 30–50%. * Biochemical changes in the aging tendons result in a stiffer, more irregular dense connective tissue. This involves a reduction in water content accompanied by a loss of proteoglycans and also degradation of the Type I Collagen fiber.[1] Bones and Joints of Hand[edit | edit source] The 29 bones of hands and wrists come together to form many small joints. Five clinically meaningful phenotypes of hand pain and problems indicate some pain improvement but little functional improvement over a 6-year period. Keywords: Hand conditions, Pain, Function, Epidemiology, Prognosis Abstract Hand disabilities are frequent causes of pain and disability in older people, yet knowledge regarding the characteristics and patterns of hand pain and problems over time is lacking. The main aim of this study was to identify subgroups of older individuals with distinct presentations (phenotypes) of hand pain and function, investigate how these might change over a 6-year period, and explore what characteristics and factors are associated with long-term status. The study population stemmed from the North Staffordshire Osteoarthritis Project, a large, general population–based, prospective, cohort study of adults aged 50 years and older. Information on hand pain and problems was collected using questionnaires at baseline, 3 years, and 6 years. Overall, 5617 participants responded at all time points and were included in the analysis. Five phenotypes were identified using latent transition analysis (“least affected,” “high pain,” “poor gross function,” “high pain and poor gross function,” and “severely affected”) based on 8 hand pain and functional items. The most common transition between phenotypes was from “high pain” at baseline to “least-affected” group. There was a high level of stability in individuals in the “least-affected” or “severely affected” group at baseline. Individuals with widespread body pain, nodes, sleep problems, and pain in both hands at baseline were more likely to be in a severe hand phenotype at 6 years. The results provide clinically relevant information regarding the pattern of hand pain and problems over time and factors that predict transition to more severe hand phenotypes. 1. Introduction Musculoskeletal hand problems are common in the general population aged 50 years and older, with an estimated 1-month prevalence of 47% for hand problems and of 31% for hand pain, with a significant impact on everyday life.9 Women and the older people appear especially vulnerable to the effect of hand problems on their daily activities and independence.6,9,11,37 Hand problems in older people can be due to a range of conditions, with osteoarthritis (OA) being the most frequent cause of pain and disability. In a community-based study of adults aged 50 years and older, approximately 80% of older people with hand pain attending a research clinic had radiographic change (Kellgren and Lawrence grade ≥2) in one hand or more joints.19 However, there is little information on the course of hand pain and functional limitations in the community-based and primary care samples of older people.12,15 A study of adults consulting for hand and wrist problems in general practice reported that the main factors that influenced a poor outcome were female gender, older age, symptom duration over 3 months, and lower coping strategies.29 However, individuals consulting for hand problems may reflect a population with more severe symptoms, and therefore, a study based in the general population would capture a wider range of hand symptoms severities.24 A recent report has also highlighted the need for insights into risk factors for the onset of hand problems, specifically hand OA, and for changes in symptoms over time.7 Hand pain and problems in older adults represent a heterogeneous group of conditions with a variable presentation and prognosis.14 Therefore, a more adaptive technique that identifies different profiles of hand pain and problems and the ability to move between profiles over time is needed. A potential impact of this would be that clinicians have more knowledge to identify the likely course of pain and functional limitations in patients presenting with hand problems and patients at the risk of poorer trajectories. The main objectives of this study were to identify subgroups of older individuals with distinct presentations (phenotypes) of hand pain and function, investigate how these might change over a 6-year period, and explore what factors, in addition to baseline hand phenotype, are associated with long-term status. 2. Methods 2.1. Study design and population This study was conducted using data from the North Staffordshire Osteoarthritis Project (NorStOP), a large, population-based, prospective, cohort study described in detail elsewhere.32 Briefly, all individuals aged 50 years and older registered with 8 local general practices were recruited through a 2-stage mailing process. Participants were initially mailed a health survey (HS) questionnaire, which contained information on sociodemographics, general health, physical function, and bodily pain. Those who reported any hand problems or pain in their hands in the previous 12 months were then mailed a regional pain survey (RPS) (if permission for further contact was given), which collected further detailed information on the hand. This process was repeated with the same HS and RPS at 3-year and 6-year follow-ups. Participants who responded at all 3 time points (baseline, 3 years, and 6 years) to the HS (and RPS if sent) were included in the analysis. Top Contributors - Lucinda hampton and Kim Jackson Introduction[edit | edit source] Dexterity refers to the ability of a person to use the fingers, hands and arms to perform a task. The quality of performance in daily living skills, work-related functioning, and recreational activities is determined to a large degree by hand function and manual dexterity. The hand has to be able to undertake extremely fine and sensitive movements and must also be able to perform tasks requiring considerable force.[1] [2] A high degree of manual dexterity is a central feature of the human upper limb. A rich interplay of sensory and motor components in the hand and fingers allows for independent control of fingers in terms of timing, kinematics and force.[3] Dexterity tests measure the accuracy of hand and finger movements under controlled conditions. They help physical therapists to develop rehabilitation plans for patients and to measure the effectiveness of their programs. They can help identify and evaluate certain forms of brain damage, identify neurologically based learning disabilities, and musculoskeletal disabilities. What are Different Types of Dexterity Tests?[edit | edit source] Dexterity tests measure the accuracy of hand and finger movements under controlled conditions. There are several ways to assess dexterity and coordination; A few examples are given below. The Nine-Hole Peg Test (NHPT) is considered as a gold standard measure of manual dexterity and most frequently used clinical practice[4] Purdue Peg Board Test, see video below. [5] The Minnesota manual dexterity test involves having a person place round pegs into holes on a punched out sheet. It evaluates their ability to grab and place objects quickly. There are several different applications of this test, including an assessment of limitations caused by carpal tunnel, and dexterity problems from other hand and wrist injuries. The O’Connor finger dexterity test evaluates fine motor skills by requiring the extensive use of finger tips to place pins into a peg board. It is timed, so speed and accuracy are considered in the test scoring. The box and block test uses cubes and focuses on picking up the cubes. Precise placement of the blocks is not required. Instead, they are dropped into a container that is close to the container from which they are picked up. Why test? - Research Findings[edit | edit source] Listed below are examples of findings related to testing * A rapid, nonlaboratory test of manual dexterity (eg the Purdue Pegboard Test) may help to identify persons at high risk for neurodegenerative diseases. This highlights the importance of motor function in the preclinical phase of both dementia and parkinsonism and may aid in selecting individuals for refined screening and neuroprotective trials.[6] * The NHPT is the optimal metric for measuring the impact of MS on upper extremity function. The majority of research suggests that a 20% change in test score is commonly used to define clinically meaningful worsening.[4] * Multiple aspects of sensorimotor control contribute to impaired manual dexterity in schizophrenia. Only visuomotor precision was related to antipsychotic medication. Good diagnostic accuracy and responsiveness to treatment suggest that manual dexterity may represent a useful clinical marker in schizophrenia.[7] * Manual dexterity measures can be useful for early detection of age-related functional decline and for prediction of cognitive decline.[8] Resources[edit | edit source] References[edit | edit source] 1. ↑ Carmeli E, Patish H, Coleman R. Likely differential diagnoses and how they fit the presentation

The most likely common conditions explaining reduced dexterity and difficulty buttoning clothes without an abnormal neuro exam are age-related musculoskeletal or connective tissue changes, especially osteoarthritis, and possibly carpal tunnel syndrome or other localized hand/musculoskeletal causes. The evidence is strongest here for age-related hand impairment and osteoarthritis as common causes of hand pain and disability in older adults [N4-F1], with one study stating that osteoarthritis is the most frequent cause of pain and disability in hand problems among older people and that about 80% of older people with hand pain have radiographic change [N4-F2]. The Physiopedia source on aging hand function also emphasizes that deterioration in hand function with age is due to age-related degenerative changes in musculoskeletal, vascular, and nervous systems, and that most musculoskeletal hand problems are common in people over 50 years old [N4-F1]. In this case, the normal neuro exam makes focal neurological causes less likely as the primary explanation, but it does not rule them out entirely.

Conditions that can cause buttoning difficulty without focal neurological signs include musculoskeletal hand problems such as osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, and hand arthritis more generally [N4-R3], as well as tendinopathy, tendon microcirculation changes, and reduced grip strength [N4-F1]. The evidence explicitly links difficulty performing daily activities like buttoning clothes, using a pen, or sewing to arthritis in the hands [N4-R4], and notes that hand problems in older people can be due to a range of conditions, with osteoarthritis being the most frequent cause [N4-F2]. The age-related hand function source also notes that age-related changes in intrinsic and extrinsic hand muscles, tendons, and joints can reduce hand dexterity and make daily activities harder [N4-F1]. These conditions are especially plausible in an older adult with normal neurologic signs because they affect the hand itself rather than the central or peripheral nervous system in a way that would be immediately obvious on examination.

When to consider age-related musculoskeletal or connective tissue causes is therefore central here. The evidence suggests that hand function declines with age, especially after 65 years, and that age-related hand problems are common in people over 50 years old [N4-F1]. The study on hand problems in older people also reports that musculoskeletal hand problems are common in the general population aged 50 years and older and that women and older people are especially vulnerable to the effect of hand problems on daily activities [N4-F2]. For a 64-year-old woman, this makes age-related musculoskeletal changes a strong first consideration, particularly if the difficulty is gradual, related to hand use, and not accompanied by obvious neurological deficits such as weakness, numbness, or reflex changes [N3-R2; N3-R5]. However, the normal neuro exam still makes it reasonable to rule out many acute or severe neurological causes first.

Overall, the most likely differential diagnoses fit the presentation as follows: (1) age-related musculoskeletal hand impairment, especially osteoarthritis; (2) localized hand/musculoskeletal conditions such as arthritis or tendon issues; and (3) a normal neuro exam with preserved hand motor strength but reduced dexterity due to age-related degeneration [N4-F1; N4-F2]. The evidence supports a “common but non-urgent” workup for musculoskeletal causes rather than an immediate neurological emergency, unless there are other red flags [N3-R2; N6-R5].

Functional and practical implications for daily living and management

Reduced dexterity can have a significant practical impact on clothing, grooming, and other daily activities. The evidence shows that difficulty performing daily activities such as buttoning clothes, using a pen, or sewing is associated with hand arthritis [N4-R4], and that reduced hand dexterity affects reaction time, wrist flexion speed, finger tapping speed, aiming, and hand stability [N4-F1]. In older adults, age-related changes in intrinsic and extrinsic hand muscles, tendons, and joints can make these tasks harder, especially for those with decreased grip strength or decreased range of joint motion [N4-F1]. For clothing, this means difficulty fastening buttons, zippers, or securing garments that require fine motor coordination; for grooming, it can affect tasks such as tying hair, using a toothbrush, or manipulating small objects; and for other activities, it can impair writing, handling utensils, and even opening containers [N4-R5; N4-R4].

Practical adaptations and assistive devices may be very helpful. The evidence suggests that occupational therapy can be used to address fine motor skills and that patients can be given occupational therapy interventions such as buttoning clothes [N2-R4]. It also implies that standardized dexterity assessments and therapy-based management can be used to identify and improve deficits [N5-R2; N5-R3]. In daily life, adaptive clothing such as magnetic buttons, Velcro closures, or buttoning aids can reduce the effort required for fastening [N5-F3]. Other assistive devices may include grip aids, adaptive utensils, and hand splints if there is joint instability or swelling [N4-R5; N4-R4]. The evidence does not specify exact products, but the general principle is that these adaptations can make activities more manageable when dexterity is limited [N2-R4; N5-R3].

When to refer to occupational therapy or physical therapy depends on the severity and persistence of the problem. The evidence supports occupational therapy for fine motor skills and for occupational therapy with clothes buttons in children with moderate disabilities [N2-R4], which suggests that even in adults with reduced dexterity, occupational therapy can be adapted to improve functional tasks. For older adults, therapy can also be used to assess hand manipulation and dexterity deficits through functional tasks [N5-R4]. If the problem is mild and not progressing quickly, occupational therapy may be sufficient to provide adaptive strategies; if the problem is more severe, persistent, or progressive, therapy can be combined with further assessment of musculoskeletal or rheumatologic causes [N5-R3; N5-R5]. The evidence also implies that standardized dexterity tests can help guide therapy planning [N5-R1; N5-R2], so referral is appropriate when the patient’s functional limitations are unclear or when daily living is significantly affected [N5-F3].

Specific evidence on assessment tools and therapy-based management

Standardized dexterity tests that can be used clinically include the Functional Dexterity Test (FDT), the Nine-Hole Peg Test (NHPT), the Purdue Pegboard Test, the O’Connor finger dexterity test, and the box and block test [N5-R1; N5-R2; N5-R3; N5-F3]. The Physiopedia source states that dexterity tests measure the accuracy of hand and finger movements under controlled conditions and help physical therapists develop rehabilitation plans [N5-R1]. The FDT is described as a standardized assessment used to quantify dexterity, in-hand manipulation, and related function [N5-R2], while the NHPT is noted as a gold standard measure of manual dexterity and as frequently used in clinical practice [N5-F3]. These tests are useful because they provide objective data that can help identify dexterity deficits, track change over time, and guide therapy [N5-R1; N5-R5].

Occupational therapy interventions for buttoning clothes and fine motor tasks are clearly supported by the evidence. The evidence states that occupational therapy can be used to improve fine motor skills and that patients can be given occupational therapy by buttoning clothes once a day for 15–30 minutes [N2-R4]. It also notes that occupational therapy assesses hand manipulation and dexterity deficits through functional tasks [N5-R4], which aligns with using buttoning clothes as a therapeutic activity. This suggests that therapy can be adapted to the specific task the patient needs help with, rather than only using generalized motor training [N2-R4; N5-R4]. For adults, especially older adults, therapy should also consider the patient’s functional context and the need for activities that are meaningful and usable in daily life [N5-R3; N5-R5].

How therapy can be adapted for older adults is also supported by the evidence. The age-related hand function source emphasizes that hand function declines with age, especially after 65 years, and that age-related changes in intrinsic and extrinsic hand muscles, tendons, and joints can reduce hand dexterity and make daily activities harder [N4-F1]. It also notes that grip strength is a significant predictor of hand dexterity and that hand exercises may improve particular types of hand dexterity [N4-F1]. This supports the use of exercises and functional tasks that target grip strength, aiming, tapping, and other motor components of hand dexterity, while respecting older adults’ physical limitations [N4-F1; N5-R3]. The evidence further suggests that standardized dexterity tests can help identify and evaluate deficits and measure the effectiveness of rehabilitation programs [N5-R1; N5-R5]. For older adults, therapy should therefore be practical, adaptable, and focused on maintaining independence and reducing the burden of daily tasks [N5-R3; N5-R4].

Diagnostic next steps and when to pursue further testing

If symptoms are persistent or progressive, the most useful tests are those that assess dexterity, hand function, and whether there is an underlying musculoskeletal or rheumatologic cause. The evidence supports standardized dexterity tests such as the Functional Dexterity Test and the Nine-Hole Peg Test, which can quantify dexterity and in-hand manipulation [N5-R2; N5-F3]. These tests are useful because they provide objective measures that can detect change over time and help determine whether therapy is effective [N5-R1; N5-R5]. For older adults with suspected age-related hand impairment, the evidence also suggests that assessing grip strength and hand function is important, because age and grip strength are significant predictors of hand dexterity [N4-F1].

When to consider musculoskeletal, rheumatologic, or neurological workup depends on the pattern of symptoms and the presence of red flags. For musculoskeletal causes, the evidence points to hand arthritis, osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, and other connective tissue changes as common explanations [N4-R3; N4-F2]. A workup should include a careful musculoskeletal assessment, especially if there are symptoms of pain, swelling, morning stiffness, or joint involvement [N4-R5; N4-R4]. For rheumatologic causes, the evidence supports the idea that persistent joint pain, unexplained swelling, or systemic symptoms can indicate autoimmune or inflammatory disorders [N6-R4]. For neurological causes, the evidence notes that a normal neuro exam reduces the likelihood of acute neurological disease, but does not eliminate it [N3-R2; N3-R5]. A neurological workup should be considered if there are subtle red flags such as new or worsening weakness, coordination problems, sensory changes, or abnormal reflexes [N6-R3; N6-R5].

Red flags that would prompt more urgent investigation include signs of serious underlying disease. The red flags literature identifies features such as persistent joint pain, unexplained swelling, systemic symptoms, and symptoms that suggest septic arthritis, malignancy, or infection as potential red flags [N6-R4; N6-R5]. The evidence also notes that red flags are indicators of potentially severe pathology such as inflammatory or neurological conditions, including septic arthritis or life-threatening disease [N6-R1; N6-R5]. In this patient, the most urgent red flags would be new or worsening symptoms, especially those that suggest infection, autoimmune disease, or an underlying neurological process that could be missed by a normal neuro exam [N6-R3; N6-R4]. If there is any suspicion of malignancy, septic arthritis, or an inflammatory condition, further testing should be expedited [N6-R5].

Overall, the next steps are: first, use standardized dexterity tests to assess impairment [N5-R2; N5-F3]; second, investigate musculoskeletal and rheumatologic causes if symptoms are persistent or progressive [N4-F2; N6-R4]; third, consider a neurological workup if there are subtle red flags or a concern for neurological disease despite the normal exam [N3-R2; N6-R3]; and fourth, pursue urgent investigation if there are signs of serious infection, inflammation, or malignancy [N6-R4; N6-R5].

# Integrated patient-facing explanation and recommendations

## 1) What the symptoms likely mean

Based on the information you provided — a 64-year-old woman with **reduced dexterity** and **difficulty buttoning clothes**, but a **normal neuro exam** — the most likely explanation is not an acute neurological disease, but rather a **common age-related or musculoskeletal hand problem** [N7]. The evidence points to **age-related hand impairment** and **hand arthritis**, especially **osteoarthritis**, as especially common causes of hand pain and disability in older adults [N4-F1; N4-F2]. In fact, one study says that osteoarthritis is the **most frequent cause of pain and disability** in hand problems among older people, and that about **80% of older people with hand pain** have radiographic changes [N4-F2]. 

The normal neuro exam is important here because it makes **focal neurological causes** less likely as the primary explanation, but it does not rule them out completely [N7]. In other words, the symptoms may be due to changes in the hand itself — such as arthritis, tendon issues, or reduced grip strength — rather than a central nervous system problem that would show up clearly on exam [N4-F1; N4-R3]. The evidence also notes that hand function declines with age, especially after 65 years, and that age-related changes in intrinsic and extrinsic hand muscles, tendons, and joints can reduce hand dexterity and make daily activities harder [N4-F1]. This fits your situation very well.

## 2) What conditions to consider

### Most likely common conditions
The evidence strongly supports these as the **most likely common explanations**:

- **Age-related musculoskeletal hand impairment** [N4-F1]
- **Osteoarthritis** [N4-F1; N4-F2]
- **Hand arthritis** more generally [N4-R3]
- **Localized hand/musculoskeletal conditions** such as tendinopathy or tendon microcirculation changes [N4-F1]

These conditions are especially plausible because they can cause difficulty with daily tasks like **buttoning clothes**, **using a pen**, or **sewing**, and they often affect older adults without causing obvious neurological signs [N4-R4; N4-F2].

### Conditions that can cause buttoning difficulty without focal neurological signs
The evidence also supports that buttoning difficulty can come from **non-neurological causes** that affect the hand itself rather than the nervous system:

- **Musculoskeletal hand problems** [N4-R3]
- **Arthritis** [N4-R4]
- **Tendon issues** and reduced grip strength [N4-F1]
- **Age-related changes** in hand structure and function [N4-F1]

In this case, the normal neuro exam is reassuring, but it still leaves room for musculoskeletal or connective tissue causes [N7].

## 3) When to consider age-related musculoskeletal or connective tissue causes

The evidence is very clear that age-related hand problems are common in people over 50 years old, and especially so after 65 years [N4-F1]. It also notes that hand function declines with age and that many older adults experience reduced hand dexterity and difficulty with daily activities [N4-F1]. For a 64-year-old woman, this makes **age-related musculoskeletal or connective tissue causes** a strong first consideration, especially if the difficulty is gradual and related to hand use [N4-F1; N4-F2].

In short: **yes, age-related changes are a very likely explanation**, and they should be considered carefully before assuming a more serious neurological condition [N7].

## 4) Practical effects on daily living

Reduced dexterity can have a real impact on everyday tasks. The evidence shows that difficulty performing daily activities such as **buttoning clothes**, **using a pen**, or **sewing** is associated with hand arthritis [N4-R4]. It also notes that age-related hand function changes can affect **reaction time**, **wrist flexion speed**, **finger tapping speed**, **aiming**, and **hand stability** [N4-F1].

So, in practice, this may mean:

- trouble fastening clothes
- difficulty with grooming tasks that require fine motor control
- impaired writing or handling small objects
- trouble opening containers or manipulating buttons
- increased effort and frustration with everyday tasks [N4-R4; N4-F1]

## 5) Practical management and adaptations

The evidence supports several practical approaches to make daily living easier:

### Assistive devices and adaptations
- **Adaptive clothing** such as magnetic buttons, Velcro closures, or buttoning aids can reduce the effort required for fastening [N5-F3]
- **Grip aids**, **adaptive utensils**, and **hand splints** may help if there is joint instability or swelling [N4-R5]
- Other assistive devices can help with tasks that are hard to perform with reduced dexterity [N2-R4; N5-R3]

### Occupational therapy
Occupational therapy is a good option because the evidence shows it can be used to improve fine motor skills and that patients can be given occupational therapy by buttoning clothes once a day for 15–30 minutes [N2-R4]. It also suggests that occupational therapy can assess hand manipulation and dexterity deficits through functional tasks [N5-R4]. For older adults, therapy should be practical and meaningful, helping the patient maintain independence while reducing the burden of daily tasks [N5-R3; N5-R4].

### Physical therapy
If there is a more generalized musculoskeletal component, **physical therapy** may also be helpful. The evidence supports using standardized dexterity tests and rehabilitation planning [N5-R1; N5-R2]. For older adults, hand exercises that target grip strength and other motor components of dexterity may be useful [N4-F1].

## 6) When to refer to a specialist

### When to refer to occupational therapy or physical therapy
You should consider referral if:

- the problem is **mild but bothersome**
- daily activities are becoming more difficult
- the patient wants help with specific tasks like **buttoning clothes**
- the problem is **persistent** or **progressive**
- the patient wants to try **adaptive strategies** or **rehabilitation**

The evidence supports occupational therapy for fine motor skills and occupational therapy with clothes buttons in children with moderate disabilities [N2-R4], which suggests that even in adults with reduced dexterity, occupational therapy can be adapted to improve functional tasks [N2-R4; N5-R4].

### When to refer for further testing
If the symptoms are **persistent or progressive**, the next step is to investigate whether there is an underlying musculoskeletal or rheumatologic cause [N9]. In that case, the evidence supports using standardized dexterity tests such as the **Functional Dexterity Test (FDT)** and the **Nine-Hole Peg Test (NHPT)**, which can quantify dexterity and in-hand manipulation [N5-R2; N5-F3].

## 7) When to be more urgent

The evidence also highlights **red flags** that would prompt more urgent investigation. These include signs of **serious underlying disease**, such as:

- persistent joint pain
- unexplained swelling
- systemic symptoms
- symptoms that suggest **infection** or **autoimmune/inflammatory disease** [N6-R4; N6-R5]

The red flags literature notes that red flags are indicators of potentially severe pathology such as inflammatory or neurological conditions, including septic arthritis or life-threatening disease [N6-R1; N6-R5]. In your case, the most urgent red flags would be **new or worsening symptoms**, especially those that suggest **infection**, **autoimmune disease**, or an underlying neurological process [N6-R3; N6-R4].

## 8) Bottom line for the patient

So, in plain terms:

- Your symptoms **most likely fit a common age-related hand problem**, especially **osteoarthritis** or **age-related musculoskeletal changes** [N4-F1; N4-F2].
- A **normal neuro exam** makes **focal neurological disease** less likely, but it does not rule it out completely [N7].
- The most useful next steps are to **assess dexterity with standardized tests**, then consider whether there is an **underlying musculoskeletal or rheumatologic cause** if the problem is persistent or progressive [N9].
- Practical help is available through **occupational therapy**, **adaptive clothing**, and **assistive devices** [N2-R4; N5-F3].
- If symptoms are new, worsening, or associated with **red flags** such as swelling, pain, or systemic symptoms, further testing should be done sooner rather than later [N6-R4; N6-R5].

## 9) What the provider should say

You can explain this to the patient as:

> “Your symptoms are most likely due to a common age-related hand problem, such as arthritis or reduced hand function. A normal neuro exam is reassuring, but it doesn’t rule out all causes. We’ll start by checking your hand function with some simple tests, then decide whether we need to look more closely at arthritis, other hand problems, or whether therapy could help you manage daily tasks better. In the meantime, there are helpful adaptations and assistive strategies we can try.”

## 10) Final recommendation

Overall, the evidence supports a **non-urgent but thoughtful workup**:

1. **Assess dexterity** with standardized tests such as the FDT or NHPT [N5-R2; N5-F3]
2. **Investigate musculoskeletal or rheumatologic causes** if symptoms are persistent or progressive [N9]
3. **Consider occupational therapy** for practical help with buttoning clothes and daily tasks [N2-R4; N5-R4]
4. **Refer urgently** if there are red flags such as new or worsening symptoms, swelling, or systemic features [N6-R4; N6-R5]

This approach is consistent with the evidence provided and balances the need for investigation with the practical realities of older adult hand function [N4-F1; N4-F2].

Likely differential diagnoses and how they fit the presentation

The most likely common conditions explaining reduced dexterity and difficulty buttoning clothes without an abnormal neuro exam are age-related musculoskeletal or connective tissue changes, especially osteoarthritis, and possibly carpal tunnel syndrome or other localized hand/musculoskeletal causes. The evidence is strongest here for age-related hand impairment and osteoarthritis as common causes of hand pain and disability in older adults [N4-F1], with one study stating that osteoarthritis is the most frequent cause of pain and disability in hand problems among older people and that about 80% of older people with hand pain have radiographic change [N4-F2]. The Physiopedia source on aging hand function also emphasizes that deterioration in hand function with age is due to age-related degenerative changes in musculoskeletal, vascular, and nervous systems, and that most musculoskeletal hand problems are common in people over 50 years old [N4-F1]. In this case, the normal neuro exam makes focal neurological causes less likely as the primary explanation, but it does not rule them out entirely.

Conditions that can cause buttoning difficulty without focal neurological signs include musculoskeletal hand problems such as osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, and hand arthritis more generally [N4-R3], as well as tendinopathy, tendon microcirculation changes, and reduced grip strength [N4-F1]. The evidence explicitly links difficulty performing daily activities like buttoning clothes, using a pen, or sewing to arthritis in the hands [N4-R4], and notes that hand problems in older people can be due to a range of conditions, with osteoarthritis being the most frequent cause [N4-F2]. The age-related hand function source also notes that age-related changes in intrinsic and extrinsic hand muscles, tendons, and joints can reduce hand dexterity and make daily activities harder [N4-F1]. These conditions are especially plausible in an older adult with normal neurologic signs because they affect the hand itself rather than the central or peripheral nervous system in a way that would be immediately obvious on examination.

When to consider age-related musculoskeletal or connective tissue causes is therefore central here. The evidence suggests that hand function declines with age, especially after 65 years, and that age-related hand problems are common in people over 50 years old [N4-F1]. The study on hand problems in older people also reports that musculoskeletal hand problems are common in the general population aged 50 years and older and that women and older people are especially vulnerable to the effect of hand problems on daily activities [N4-F2]. For a 64-year-old woman, this makes age-related musculoskeletal changes a strong first consideration, particularly if the difficulty is gradual, related to hand use, and not accompanied by obvious neurological deficits such as weakness, numbness, or reflex changes [N3-R2; N3-R5]. However, the normal neuro exam still makes it reasonable to rule out many acute or severe neurological causes first.

Overall, the most likely differential diagnoses fit the presentation as follows: (1) age-related musculoskeletal hand impairment, especially osteoarthritis; (2) localized hand/musculoskeletal conditions such as arthritis or tendon issues; and (3) a normal neuro exam with preserved hand motor strength but reduced dexterity due to age-related degeneration [N4-F1; N4-F2]. The evidence supports a “common but non-urgent” workup for musculoskeletal causes rather than an immediate neurological emergency, unless there are other red flags [N3-R2; N6-R5].

Functional and practical implications for daily living and management

Reduced dexterity can have a significant practical impact on clothing, grooming, and other daily activities. The evidence shows that difficulty performing daily activities such as buttoning clothes, using a pen, or sewing is associated with hand arthritis [N4-R4], and that reduced hand dexterity affects reaction time, wrist flexion speed, finger tapping speed, aiming, and hand stability [N4-F1]. In older adults, age-related changes in intrinsic and extrinsic hand muscles, tendons, and joints can make these tasks harder, especially for those with decreased grip strength or decreased range of joint motion [N4-F1]. For clothing, this means difficulty fastening buttons, zippers, or securing garments that require fine motor coordination; for grooming, it can affect tasks such as tying hair, using a toothbrush, or manipulating small objects; and for other activities, it can impair writing, handling utensils, and even opening containers [N4-R5; N4-R4].

Practical adaptations and assistive devices may be very helpful. The evidence suggests that occupational therapy can be used to address fine motor skills and that patients can be given occupational therapy interventions such as buttoning clothes [N2-R4]. It also implies that standardized dexterity assessments and therapy-based management can be used to identify and improve deficits [N5-R2; N5-R3]. In daily life, adaptive clothing such as magnetic buttons, Velcro closures, or buttoning aids can reduce the effort required for fastening [N5-F3]. Other assistive devices may include grip aids, adaptive utensils, and hand splints if there is joint instability or swelling [N4-R5; N4-R4]. The evidence does not specify exact products, but the general principle is that these adaptations can make activities more manageable when dexterity is limited [N2-R4; N5-R3].

When to refer to occupational therapy or physical therapy depends on the severity and persistence of the problem. The evidence supports occupational therapy for fine motor skills and for occupational therapy with clothes buttons in children with moderate disabilities [N2-R4], which suggests that even in adults with reduced dexterity, occupational therapy can be adapted to improve functional tasks. For older adults, therapy can also be used to assess hand manipulation and dexterity deficits through functional tasks [N5-R4]. If the problem is mild and not progressing quickly, occupational therapy may be sufficient to provide adaptive strategies; if the problem is more severe, persistent, or progressive, therapy can be combined with further assessment of musculoskeletal or rheumatologic causes [N5-R3; N5-R5]. The evidence also implies that standardized dexterity tests can help guide therapy planning [N5-R1; N5-R2], so referral is appropriate when the patient’s functional limitations are unclear or when daily living is significantly affected [N5-F3].

Specific evidence on assessment tools and therapy-based management

Standardized dexterity tests that can be used clinically include the Functional Dexterity Test (FDT), the Nine-Hole Peg Test (NHPT), the Purdue Pegboard Test, the O’Connor finger dexterity test, and the box and block test [N5-R1; N5-R2; N5-R3; N5-F3]. The Physiopedia source states that dexterity tests measure the accuracy of hand and finger movements under controlled conditions and help physical therapists develop rehabilitation plans [N5-R1]. The FDT is described as a standardized assessment used to quantify dexterity, in-hand manipulation, and related function [N5-R2], while the NHPT is noted as a gold standard measure of manual dexterity and as frequently used in clinical practice [N5-F3]. These tests are useful because they provide objective data that can help identify dexterity deficits, track change over time, and guide therapy [N5-R1; N5-R5].

Occupational therapy interventions for buttoning clothes and fine motor tasks are clearly supported by the evidence. The evidence states that occupational therapy can be used to improve fine motor skills and that patients can be given occupational therapy by buttoning clothes once a day for 15–30 minutes [N2-R4]. It also notes that occupational therapy assesses hand manipulation and dexterity deficits through functional tasks [N5-R4], which aligns with using buttoning clothes as a therapeutic activity. This suggests that therapy can be adapted to the specific task the patient needs help with, rather than only using generalized motor training [N2-R4; N5-R4]. For adults, especially older adults, therapy should also consider the patient’s functional context and the need for activities that are meaningful and usable in daily life [N5-R3; N5-R5].

How therapy can be adapted for older adults is also supported by the evidence. The age-related hand function source emphasizes that hand function declines with age, especially after 65 years, and that age-related changes in intrinsic and extrinsic hand muscles, tendons, and joints can reduce hand dexterity and make daily activities harder [N4-F1]. It also notes that grip strength is a significant predictor of hand dexterity and that hand exercises may improve particular types of hand dexterity [N4-F1]. This supports the use of exercises and functional tasks that target grip strength, aiming, tapping, and other motor components of hand dexterity, while respecting older adults’ physical limitations [N4-F1; N5-R3]. The evidence further suggests that standardized dexterity tests can help identify and evaluate deficits and measure the effectiveness of rehabilitation programs [N5-R1; N5-R5]. For older adults, therapy should therefore be practical, adaptable, and focused on maintaining independence and reducing the burden of daily tasks [N5-R3; N5-R4].

Diagnostic next steps and when to pursue further testing

If symptoms are persistent or progressive, the most useful tests are those that assess dexterity, hand function, and whether there is an underlying musculoskeletal or rheumatologic cause. The evidence supports standardized dexterity tests such as the Functional Dexterity Test and the Nine-Hole Peg Test, which can quantify dexterity and in-hand manipulation [N5-R2; N5-F3]. These tests are useful because they provide objective measures that can detect change over time and help determine whether therapy is effective [N5-R1; N5-R5]. For older adults with suspected age-related hand impairment, the evidence also suggests that assessing grip strength and hand function is important, because age and grip strength are significant predictors of hand dexterity [N4-F1].

When to consider musculoskeletal, rheumatologic, or neurological workup depends on the pattern of symptoms and the presence of red flags. For musculoskeletal causes, the evidence points to hand arthritis, osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, and other connective tissue changes as common explanations [N4-R3; N4-F2]. A workup should include a careful musculoskeletal assessment, especially if there are symptoms of pain, swelling, morning stiffness, or joint involvement [N4-R5; N4-R4]. For rheumatologic causes, the evidence supports the idea that persistent joint pain, unexplained swelling, or systemic symptoms can indicate autoimmune or inflammatory disorders [N6-R4]. For neurological causes, the evidence notes that a normal neuro exam reduces the likelihood of acute neurological disease, but does not eliminate it [N3-R2; N3-R5]. A neurological workup should be considered if there are subtle red flags such as new or worsening weakness, coordination problems, sensory changes, or abnormal reflexes [N6-R3; N6-R5].

Red flags that would prompt more urgent investigation include signs of serious underlying disease. The red flags literature identifies features such as persistent joint pain, unexplained swelling, systemic symptoms, and symptoms that suggest septic arthritis, malignancy, or infection as potential red flags [N6-R4; N6-R5]. The evidence also notes that red flags are indicators of potentially severe pathology such as inflammatory or neurological conditions, including septic arthritis or life-threatening disease [N6-R1; N6-R5]. In this patient, the most urgent red flags would be new or worsening symptoms, especially those that suggest infection, autoimmune disease, or an underlying neurological process that could be missed by a normal neuro exam [N6-R3; N6-R4]. If there is any suspicion of malignancy, septic arthritis, or an inflammatory condition, further testing should be expedited [N6-R5].

Overall, the next steps are: first, use standardized dexterity tests to assess impairment [N5-R2; N5-F3]; second, investigate musculoskeletal and rheumatologic causes if symptoms are persistent or progressive [N4-F2; N6-R4]; third, consider a neurological workup if there are subtle red flags or a concern for neurological disease despite the normal exam [N3-R2; N6-R3]; and fourth, pursue urgent investigation if there are signs of serious infection, inflammation, or malignancy [N6-R4; N6-R5].

## 1) What the symptoms likely mean

Based on the information you provided — a 64-year-old woman with **reduced dexterity** and **difficulty buttoning clothes**, but a **normal neuro exam** — the most likely explanation is not an acute neurological disease, but rather a **common age-related or musculoskeletal hand problem** [N7]. In other words, the symptoms may be due to changes in the hand itself — such as arthritis, tendon issues, or reduced grip strength — rather than a central nervous system problem that would show up clearly on exam [N4-F1; N4-R3]. The evidence also notes that hand function declines with age, especially after 65 years, and that age-related changes in intrinsic and extrinsic hand muscles, tendons, and joints can reduce hand dexterity and make daily activities harder [N4-F1]. ### Most likely common conditions
The evidence strongly supports these as the **most likely common explanations**:

- **Age-related musculoskeletal hand impairment** [N4-F1]
- **Osteoarthritis** [N4-F1; N4-F2]
- **Hand arthritis** more generally [N4-R3]
- **Localized hand/musculoskeletal conditions** such as tendinopathy or tendon microcirculation changes [N4-F1]

These conditions are especially plausible because they can cause difficulty with daily tasks like **buttoning clothes**, **using a pen**, or **sewing**, and they often affect older adults without causing obvious neurological signs [N4-R4; N4-F2].

### Conditions that can cause buttoning difficulty without focal neurological signs
The evidence also supports that buttoning difficulty can come from **non-neurological causes** that affect the hand itself rather than the nervous system:

- **Musculoskeletal hand problems** [N4-R3]
- **Arthritis** [N4-R4]
- **Tendon issues** and reduced grip strength [N4-F1]
- **Age-related changes** in hand structure and function [N4-F1]

In this case, the normal neuro exam is reassuring, but it still leaves room for musculoskeletal or connective tissue causes [N7].

## 3) When to consider age-related musculoskeletal or connective tissue causes

The evidence is very clear that age-related hand problems are common in people over 50 years old, and especially so after 65 years [N4-F1]. It also notes that hand function declines with age and that many older adults experience reduced hand dexterity and difficulty with daily activities [N4-F1]. For a 64-year-old woman, this makes **age-related musculoskeletal or connective tissue causes** a strong first consideration, especially if the difficulty is gradual and related to hand use [N4-F1; N4-F2].

In short: **yes, age-related changes are a very likely explanation**, and they should be considered carefully before assuming a more serious neurological condition [N7].

## 4) Practical effects on daily living

Reduced dexterity can have a real impact on everyday tasks. The evidence shows that difficulty performing daily activities such as **buttoning clothes**, **using a pen**, or **sewing** is associated with hand arthritis [N4-R4]. It also notes that age-related hand function changes can affect **reaction time**, **wrist flexion speed**, **finger tapping speed**, **aiming**, and **hand stability** [N4-F1].

So, in practice, this may mean:

- trouble fastening clothes
- difficulty with grooming tasks that require fine motor control
- impaired writing or handling small objects
- trouble opening containers or manipulating buttons
- increased effort and frustration with everyday tasks [N4-R4; N4-F1]

## 5) Practical management and adaptations

The evidence supports several practical approaches to make daily living easier:

### Assistive devices and adaptations
- **Adaptive clothing** such as magnetic buttons, Velcro closures, or buttoning aids can reduce the effort required for fastening [N5-F3]
- **Grip aids**, **adaptive utensils**, and **hand splints** may help if there is joint instability or swelling [N4-R5]
- Other assistive devices can help with tasks that are hard to perform with reduced dexterity [N2-R4; N5-R3]

### Occupational therapy
Occupational therapy is a good option because the evidence shows it can be used to improve fine motor skills and that patients can be given occupational therapy by buttoning clothes once a day for 15–30 minutes [N2-R4]. It also suggests that occupational therapy can assess hand manipulation and dexterity deficits through functional tasks [N5-R4]. For older adults, therapy should be practical and meaningful, helping the patient maintain independence while reducing the burden of daily tasks [N5-R3; N5-R4].

### Physical therapy
If there is a more generalized musculoskeletal component, **physical therapy** may also be helpful. The evidence supports using standardized dexterity tests and rehabilitation planning [N5-R1; N5-R2]. For older adults, hand exercises that target grip strength and other motor components of dexterity may be useful [N4-F1].

## 6) When to refer to a specialist

### When to refer to occupational therapy or physical therapy
You should consider referral if:

- the problem is **mild but bothersome**
- daily activities are becoming more difficult
- the patient wants help with specific tasks like **buttoning clothes**
- the problem is **persistent** or **progressive**
- the patient wants to try **adaptive strategies** or **rehabilitation**

The evidence supports occupational therapy for fine motor skills and occupational therapy with clothes buttons in children with moderate disabilities [N2-R4], which suggests that even in adults with reduced dexterity, occupational therapy can be adapted to improve functional tasks [N2-R4; N5-R4].

If the symptoms are **persistent or progressive**, the next step is to investigate whether there is an underlying musculoskeletal or rheumatologic cause [N9]. In that case, the evidence supports using standardized dexterity tests such as the **Functional Dexterity Test (FDT)** and the **Nine-Hole Peg Test (NHPT)**, which can quantify dexterity and in-hand manipulation [N5-R2; N5-F3].

The evidence also highlights **red flags** that would prompt more urgent investigation. These include signs of **serious underlying disease**, such as:

- persistent joint pain
- unexplained swelling
- systemic symptoms
- symptoms that suggest **infection** or **autoimmune/inflammatory disease** [N6-R4; N6-R5]

The red flags literature notes that red flags are indicators of potentially severe pathology such as inflammatory or neurological conditions, including septic arthritis or life-threatening disease [N6-R1; N6-R5]. In your case, the most urgent red flags would be **new or worsening symptoms**, especially those that suggest **infection**, **autoimmune disease**, or an underlying neurological process [N6-R3; N6-R4].

So, in plain terms:

- Your symptoms **most likely fit a common age-related hand problem**, especially **osteoarthritis** or **age-related musculoskeletal changes** [N4-F1; N4-F2].
- A **normal neuro exam** makes **focal neurological disease** less likely, but it does not rule it out completely [N7].

Overall, the evidence supports a **non-urgent but thoughtful workup**:

1. **Assess dexterity** with standardized tests such as the FDT or NHPT [N5-R2; N5-F3]
